e.meaning: the Isle of Skye; also a spelling of sky
e.etymology: From the Isle of Skye in Scotland's Hebrides, whose Gaelic name is of disputed origin, or simply an ornamental spelling of the word sky.

assoc.t: Skye, the pink pilot pup in PAW Patrol
Isle of Skye, island in the Scottish Hebrides

e.etymology: A Maya name from Mexico, generally taken as a form of Ixchel, the Maya goddess of the moon, weaving and childbirth. Its exact meaning is debated.
The French form of Magdalene, the byname of Mary Magdalene: 'woman of Magdala', a village on the Sea of Galilee whose name means 'tower'.
namesakes: Madeleine Albright (first woman to serve as US secretary of state)
Madeleine L'Engle (author of A Wrinkle in Time)

assoc.t: madeleine, the shell-shaped French sponge cake

e.etymology: From the English word miracle, from Latin miraculum, 'object of wonder'. It is often chosen for a baby born against the odds.

assoc.t: Miracle Whip dressing; also Miracle-Gro plant food

e.meaning: Arabic form of Mary and Miriam, of uncertain meaning
e.etymology: The Arabic and Persian form of Miriam and Mary, from Aramaic Maryam. Maryam, the mother of Jesus, is the only woman named in the Quran, and its 19th chapter bears her name.
From the English word joy, from Old French joie and Latin gaudia. Puritans first used it as a given name in the 17th century.
namesakes: Joy Behar (co-host of The View)
Joy (the lead emotion in Pixar's Inside Out)
Joy Reid (political commentator and former MSNBC host)

assoc.t: Joy, the sunny lead emotion in Pixar's Inside Out
Almond Joy candy bar

e.etymology: From Hebrew Shelomoh, from shalom, 'peace'. Solomon, son of David, was the king of Israel famed for his wisdom and for building the First Temple.
namesakes: King Solomon (biblical king of Israel famed for his wisdom)
Solomon Northup (author of Twelve Years a Slave)

assoc.t: King Solomon, the wise king of the Bible
Solomon Islands, nation in the South Pacific

e.etymology: A spelling of Everly, an English surname from a place name, Old English eofor, 'wild boar', and leah, 'clearing'. Everly became a popular girls' name in the 2010s.

e.meaning: short form of Eleanor, Ellen and other El- names
e.etymology: A short form of Eleanor, Ellen and other names beginning with El, also given in its own right. It matches the French word elle, 'she', and rose with Elle Woods of Legally Blonde (2001).
namesakes: Elle Woods (heroine of Legally Blonde)
Elle Fanning (actress)
Elle Macpherson (Australian supermodel)

assoc.t: Elle, the fashion magazine
Elle Woods, heroine of Legally Blonde

e.meaning: from the mouth of the River Roe
e.etymology: From the Scottish surname Munro, traditionally explained as Gaelic for 'from the mouth of the Roe', a river in the north of Ireland. President James Monroe made it an American first name.

assoc.t: Marilyn Monroe, Hollywood icon
James Monroe, fifth US president
Monroe shocks and struts for cars

e.etymology: An English spelling of Irish Cian, from Old Irish cían, 'long, distant, lasting'. Kian is also a Persian name meaning 'king' or 'realm'.

e.meaning: short form of Juliana, Eliana and Liliana
e.etymology: A short form of names ending in -liana, such as Juliana, Eliana and Liliana. It also matches liana, the word for a climbing tropical vine.
A spelling of Oakley, an English surname and place name from Old English ac, 'oak', and leah, 'clearing'. The -lee spelling is used mostly for girls.

assoc.t: sounds the same as Oakley, the sunglasses brand
echoes Annie Oakley, the Wild West sharpshooter

e.etymology: A short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, 'my God is an oath', used across Italian, Spanish and German. In English it is also a spelling of Elise.

assoc.t: ELISA, a common antibody lab test

e.etymology: A pet form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. It has been given as a full name since the 16th century.
namesakes: Johnny Cash (country music legend)
Johnny Depp (actor)
Johnny Carson (longtime host of The Tonight Show)

assoc.t: Here's Johnny!, the Tonight Show and The Shining line

e.etymology: A French feminine form of Ariel, from Hebrew ariel, 'lion of God', a name the Bible uses for Jerusalem.

assoc.t: sounds like Ariel, Disney's Little Mermaid

e.etymology: A medieval pet form of John by way of Hankin, later used as a nickname for Henry, Germanic 'home ruler'. It is now given as a full name.
namesakes: Hank Aaron (baseball's home run king)
Hank Williams (country music pioneer)
Hank Hill (propane salesman of King of the Hill)

assoc.t: Hank Hill, the dad in King of the Hill
Hank Williams, country legend, and slugger Hank Aaron
Hank Schrader, the DEA agent in Breaking Bad

e.etymology: From Greek Helene, probably from a root meaning 'to shine'. Helen of Troy was the beauty whose abduction began the Trojan War; Saint Helena, mother of Constantine, spread the name among Christians.
namesakes: Helen Keller (deaf-blind author and activist)
Helen Mirren (Oscar-winning actress)
Helen of Troy (legendary beauty of Greek myth)

assoc.t: Helen of Troy, the face that launched a thousand ships
Helen Keller, deaf-blind author and activist

e.etymology: A modern American respelling of Elijah, from Hebrew Eliyahu, 'my God is Yahweh', the name of the Old Testament prophet.
A respelling of Lorelei, the rock on the Rhine where, in German legend, a siren's song lured boatmen to wreck. The Lorelai spelling comes from the mother and daughter of Gilmore Girls.
namesakes: Lorelai Gilmore (fast-talking mom of Gilmore Girls)

assoc.t: Lorelai Gilmore of Gilmore Girls

e.etymology: A modern American name, a spelling of Nyla with a final h. Nyla is of uncertain origin and is often linked to Arabic Naila, 'one who attains'.
From Hebrew Sarai, built on sar, 'chief, prince', and traditionally read as 'my princess'. In Genesis it is the first name of Abraham's wife before God renames her Sarah.
Of uncertain origin; it may be a variant of Hebrew Eliora, 'God is my light', or of Elnora. It became known through Elora Danan, the infant princess in the 1988 fantasy film Willow.

assoc.t: Elora Danan, the baby princess in the film Willow

e.etymology: A modern American coinage from Grace, Latin gratia, and the -lyn ending.
A Latinized form of Alice, which comes through Old French Adelais from Germanic Adalheid, 'noble kind'. It is the usual Spanish form of Alice.
namesakes: Alicia Keys (Grammy-winning singer and pianist)
Alicia Silverstone (star of Clueless)
Alicia Vikander (Oscar-winning actress)

e.etymology: From an Anglo-Norman surname, a nickname from Old French corb, 'crow, raven', perhaps for someone with dark hair. It may also shorten Corbinian, the name of an 8th-century Frankish saint.
namesakes: Corbin Bleu (actor, High School Musical)
Corbin Bernsen (actor, L.A. Law)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Asa, linked to an Aramaic word for 'healer, physician'. Asa was a reforming king of Judah in the Books of Kings, and the Puritans brought the name to America.
namesakes: Asa Butterfield (actor, Sex Education and Hugo)

e.etymology: The Latin form of Helen, from Greek Helene, probably from a root meaning 'to shine'. Saint Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, made it a favorite Christian name.
namesakes: Helena Bonham Carter (actress)

assoc.t: Helena, the capital of Montana
Saint Helena, Napoleon's island of exile
Helena, the My Chemical Romance song

e.etymology: From Old English Eadgar, joining ead, 'wealth, fortune', and gar, 'spear'. It was the name of a 10th-century English king, Edgar the Peaceful.
namesakes: Edgar Allan Poe (author of The Raven)
Edgar Degas (French painter of ballet dancers)
Edgar Martínez (Hall of Fame Seattle Mariners hitter)

assoc.t: the Edgar, a blunt-fringe haircut, and teens who wear it
Edgar Allan Poe, author of The Raven

e.note: The Edgar is a blunt-fringe haircut, and 'an Edgar' is slang, often mocking, for Latino teens who wear it.

e.etymology: From Greek Maia, eldest of the Pleiades and mother of Hermes; the word maia meant 'good mother' or 'nurse'. A Roman goddess Maia gave her name to the month of May. Also a spelling of Maya.

assoc.t: Maia, a star in the Pleiades cluster

e.etymology: From the holly tree, Old English holegn, whose red berries and evergreen leaves are a Christmas emblem. It has been given to girls since the early 20th century, often to those born in December.
namesakes: Holly Hunter (Oscar-winning actress)
Holly Golightly (heroine of Breakfast at Tiffany's)

assoc.t: holly, the Christmas evergreen with red berries

e.etymology: A Russian and Ukrainian pet form of Anna, from Hebrew Channah, 'grace, favor'. It is also used to anglicize Irish Áine and as a spelling of the Indian name Aanya.
namesakes: Anya Taylor-Joy (star of The Queen's Gambit)
Anya (the lost princess in the animated film Anastasia)

assoc.t: Anya Forger, the telepath girl of Spy x Family
